"Papa, I want to take arts after Class 10. History and political science."
Jagdish put down his newspaper. "Arts? Lalit, what will I tell your uncles? Everyone's son is doing science."
"I'm not everyone's son."
"If you do this, don't expect me to face the family at the wedding. You'll bring shame on all of us."
Lalit's throat tightened. "It's my life, Papa."
"Your life? Who paid for your tuition? Who sat with you all night when you had fever?" His voice cracked. "I only want what's best for you."
Lalit looked at his father's tired eyes. He did sit up all those nights. He did love him. And he was also saying: choose, or lose us.
"Can I think about it?" Lalit said quietly.
"Think. But remember what I said."
Lalit went to his room and stared at the ceiling, confused about where love ended and control began.

qa.q: What subjects does Lalit want to take?
qa.a: History and political science.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel as he stares at the ceiling?
qa.a: Lalit feels torn and confused, loving his father and grateful for his care, but pressured by the threat of shame and losing the family's approval.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next to get support?
qa.a: Lalit could talk to the school counsellor or a respected relative who could help him and his father discuss his choice calmly.

qa.q: How does Jagdish seem to see his own words?
qa.a: Jagdish seems to see them as love and duty, wanting the best for his son, without seeing how much they pressure Lalit.

grounding: It shows a teenager torn between love for his father and freedom to choose his subjects, when care comes with threats of shame.

My name is Bidisha, I'm fifteen, and I love my brother Chinmay more than almost anyone.
He taught me to ride a cycle. He brings me my favourite sweets from the station every Friday. When I was sick last year, he slept on the floor beside my bed.
He also checks my phone every night. He decides which friends I can visit. When I talked to a boy from my tuition about homework, he said, "Our family's name matters. If you shame us, I'll never speak to you again." Then he hugged me.
I don't know what to call it. It feels like love and a cage at the same time. When I try to explain it to friends, it sounds either too good or too bad.
Last week, I told our school counsellor. She listened, and then she said, "It's possible to love someone and still need your own freedom." I cried, because that was exactly it.

qa.q: What does Chinmay bring Bidisha every Friday?
qa.a: He brings Bidisha's favourite sweets from the station.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel about her brother?
qa.a: Bidisha feels deep affection for him and also trapped and confused, as if his love and control are a cage at the same time.

qa.q: What step did Bidisha take that helped?
qa.a: Bidisha told the school counsellor, who listened and named that love and the need for freedom can exist together.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see his checking and rules?
qa.a: Chinmay probably sees them as protecting the family name and Bidisha, not as control.

grounding: It shows a teenager loved and controlled by a brother through threats of shame and cutting ties, confused because care and control come together.

Gurleen, remember I told you I was dreading Sunday? I did it. I'm Himani, and I finally spoke to my parents.
They had been showing me photos of boys for a year. Every visit, another biodata. Papa said, "We know what's best." Mummy cried if I said no.
So on Sunday I sat them down, after lunch, calmly. I said, "I love you both. I'm not cutting you off. But I'll choose my own partner, and I'll decide when. Please stop sending biodatas."
Papa went silent. Mummy said, "After everything?" I stayed calm. I said, "I'll still come every Sunday. I'll still call Mummy every night. That doesn't change."
It wasn't magic. Papa didn't speak to me at dinner. But last night Mummy called, and asked about my day, not about boys.
If it had turned to threats or worse, I'd already saved a helpline number. Thank God it didn't.

qa.a: For a year.

qa.a: Himani felt nervous but steady, staying calm and loving while holding firm about the choice.

qa.a: Himani spoke calmly, named what Himani alone would decide, kept up Sunday visits and nightly calls, and had a helpline ready in case of threats.

I've lived next door to Jagdish Uncle and his son Asif for fifteen years, so I heard most of it through the open window on Sunday.
Asif had got a job offer in Hyderabad. His father wanted him to stay and join the family shop. Voices rose. Jagdish Uncle said, "If you go, don't come back asking for anything."
Then Asif spoke, and I remember how calm he sounded. "Abbu, I love you. I'm taking the job. I'll come home every month, and I'll call you every evening after the shop closes. I'm not leaving the family. I'm just choosing my work."
There was a long silence. I couldn't see their faces.
A month later, I saw Asif get out of an auto with a box of sweets and walk straight into the shop. His father didn't smile, exactly. But he took the box.
I don't know what either of them felt. But I know Asif kept coming.

qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.a: Asif seemed calm and loving, though probably nervous, firm about his decision while trying to keep the family close.

January. Yogesh told his father Santosh that he would marry Anjum, the woman he'd chosen. Santosh slammed his hand on the table, raised it toward him, and said, "Out of my house. Tonight." Yogesh's mother was crying in the kitchen doorway.
That same night, Yogesh went to his cousin's flat across town. He called a family counselling helpline from the balcony. They helped him think about staying safe and not going back alone while tempers were high.
February. He didn't cut his family off. He messaged his mother every evening. He told his father in a calm text, "I love you, Papa. I'm marrying Anjum. I'll visit when it's safe for all of us." No reply.
April. His mother met him at the temple. She held his hand for a long time. Then, in June, a short message came from Santosh: "Your mother misses you. Come for lunch Sunday. Bring her."
Yogesh read it three times before he could answer.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh go the night his father told him to leave?
qa.a: To his cousin's flat across town.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when he read his father's message in June?
qa.a: Yogesh felt overwhelmed and hopeful, reading it three times before he could answer.

qa.q: What steps did Yogesh take to stay safe and keep his boundary?
qa.a: He left that night for his cousin's flat, called a counselling helpline, stayed in contact by calm messages, and visited only when it was safe.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's mother have felt through these months?
qa.a: His mother was probably heartbroken and torn, crying at first, then meeting him at the temple and missing him.

grounding: It shows an adult son deciding his own marriage, seeking outside help and safe housing after a threat, while keeping affection and contact over months.

I'm Ganga, and when I was fifteen, I thought Tejas was my best friend. We met in a comments section under a music video. He said he was seventeen, from Pune. He was sweet. He remembered everything I told him.
After a month he said, "Let's talk on a private app, just us." Then he asked what time my parents got home. Then for photos. Then he said he'd come to my city to meet me, at the mall, alone. "Don't tell anyone. They'll ruin it."
I felt flattered and trapped at once. I didn't want to lose him. I also didn't want to go.
The next morning I told my class teacher before assembly. She listened without any shock in her face and said, "You're not to blame. You did exactly the right thing." She called my mother right then, and together they reported the account to the police cyber cell that afternoon.
I never went to the mall.

qa.a: Ganga felt flattered and trapped at once, not wanting to lose him but not wanting to go.

I'm Tarun, and for most of my first year in college, I was someone else online.
I made a profile with a better face and a better life. I said I played guitar and had lived in London. I was lonely and felt ugly and boring, and this version of me got messages. One of them was from Gurleen, from another college. We talked every night for five months.
She told me real things. Her father's illness. Her fear of failing her exams. And I answered as someone who didn't exist.
Every time she asked for a video call, I made an excuse. I told myself I wasn't hurting anyone. I wasn't asking for money.
Then one night she wrote, "You're the only person I trust completely." I sat on the hostel floor feeling sick. Whatever my reasons, I was using that trust.
I told her the truth the next day. She blocked me. She had every right to.

Pallavi, second year, came in today, shaking. For three months she has been running a fake profile, a confident young man with a gym photo and a startup, and chatting with Madhuri, a classmate she barely speaks to in real life.
She said she started it as a joke, then kept going because Madhuri was so warm, and because she herself felt invisible in class. "She tells him things she'd never tell me."

Samir, you think you're the only one who's ever been fooled? Sit. Let your Ira Phuppo tell you about my pen friend.
I was twenty. There was no internet then, only letters. A pen friend from Shillong wrote to me for two years. Such letters. Poems, pressed flowers, plans for our life. He never sent a photograph. His camera was broken, then lost, then stolen.
I told my friends I was in love. I turned down a proposal from a very nice boy because of those letters.
Then my cousin, visiting Shillong, went to the address. It was a printing press. The owner's son, fifty years old and married, had been writing to many girls.
I cried for a month. Not only for him. For myself, for being so foolish.
But Samir, I wasn't foolish. I was hopeful. Being fooled by a liar says something about him, not about you.

qa.a: It was a printing press.

qa.q: How did young Ira feel after the truth came out?
qa.a: Ira felt grief and shame, crying for a month and feeling foolish for believing him.

qa.a: Ira's cousin visited the address in Shillong and discovered it was a printing press run by a married man.

qa.q: How might the nice boy Ira turned down have felt?

The overnight bus from Bhopal reached Pune at seven in the morning, and it was raining hard. Zainab stood under the bus stand roof with her bag, waiting for Yash.
They had talked for eight months. He always had a reason not to video call: bad network, shy, then a hostel rule. But he'd promised he'd be at the stand with an umbrella.

Zainab stood shivering, surrounded by strangers, her face hot with shame. She'd told her college friends she was meeting her boyfriend. She'd lied to her parents about a "college trip."
She called her friend Farah, crying. Farah said, "Listen. You are not stupid. Someone lied to you on purpose. Go to the ticket counter and take the next bus home. I'll stay on the phone."
Zainab bought a ticket. On the long ride back, she let herself grieve.
